clue.text: Numerous Dutch rejected old go-getter

indicators.note: what is rejected is sent back, so the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: numerous means many
D is the abbreviation for Dutch
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A band of Dutch people turn their backs on a former high achiever.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first two pieces turn round together; the O for old is tacked on afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynamo is informally an energetic, forceful person who gets things done, a figurative sense taken from the electrical generator.

clue.text: Either end of dayroom providing somewhere to sleep

indicators.note: an end is a word's extremity, so only a letter at its start or finish is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of the word, one of its ends
either ... or: the word read as its partner
the other end of the word

explanation.surface: Either end of a communal lounge will do for a nap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Either end' reads as a choice of letters, but the setter wants both ends with OR written literally between them: D OR M.
explanation.definitionFit: A dorm, short for dormitory, is a shared room full of beds where people sleep.

clue.text: Siemens' corrupt adversary

indicators.note: something corrupt has been debased and altered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the German engineering company, taken as written

explanation.surface: A rival firm accuses the German giant Siemens of corruption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' reads as an adjective describing the company's rival, but it tells you to rearrange the company's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is a long-standing enemy or opponent that someone cannot seem to overcome.

clue.text: Frenchman with awfully cruel air, temperamental

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly and messily, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for Monsieur, a French title
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A moody Frenchman with a nasty manner.
explanation.walkthrough: M for Monsieur is the usual crossword Frenchman.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercurial describes someone whose moods shift suddenly and unpredictably, like quicksilver.

clue.text: Primarily ostentatious soirée comprising actors' rambling speeches?

definitions.text: Primarily ostentatious soirée comprising actors' rambling speeches?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the leading letter of each following word counts

blocks.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: A snooty description of a glitzy party full of actors' long-winded speeches.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its initials spell the answer, and read straight it describes the event.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oscars ceremony is Hollywood's showy awards night, notorious for tearful, overlong acceptance speeches.

clue.text: Wonderful, for it told us how to dance

indicators.note: letters made to dance move about and land in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Praise for a manual that taught us dance steps.
explanation.walkthrough: The long run of small words reads as a sentence, which hides that all fourteen letters are the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of this world is an idiom for something so excellent it seems beyond ordinary experience.

clue.text: Sign showing absence of growth in Italian island

indicators.note: showing an absence means something is missing, so letters are taken away

blocks.note: a sign of the zodiac
corn is a growing crop, and also a growth on the foot

explanation.surface: A sign of drought where nothing grows on an Italian island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' means a star sign here; remove the growth from its end.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is a well-known island in the Bay of Naples, off the southern Italian coast.

clue.text: Class war with no leader, revolutionary scoundrels

indicators.note: having no leader means the front letter is dropped
a revolution overturns the established order, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
the word minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A leaderless class war waged by revolutionary villains.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface makes 'revolutionary' look like an adjective for the scoundrels; it rearranges the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rascals are mischievous or dishonest people, a milder synonym for scoundrels or rogues.

clue.text: Unusually lithe thing opts to become famous

indicators.note: unusually means in an unexpected way, so the letters appear in an unexpected order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A strangely supple creature chooses a path to celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface grammar is loose, which is a hint that the three middle words are just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in the spotlight is receiving public attention, as a celebrity does on stage under the lights.

clue.text: Artist's unusual term describing mark

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters are out of their ordinary order
to describe a circle is to draw round it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
a brand is a mark burned or stamped on something

explanation.surface: A painter's odd choice of word to describe a mark on the canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line round something, so the rearranged letters wrap the mark. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt van Rijn was the great seventeenth-century Dutch painter, famous for portraits and dramatic light.

clue.text: Gum unpasteurised? Not entirely

indicators.note: not entirely means only part of the word is used, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: a run of letters from inside the word

explanation.surface: Is this chewing gum made from raw milk? Only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and the dairy surface make you think about milk; the answer is sitting inside the long word.
explanation.definitionFit: Gum and paste are both sticky substances used as adhesive to glue paper together.

clue.text: After Spain, a flight attendant losing energy – thence to Italy?

indicators.note: to lose something is to be left without it, so a letter goes

blocks.note: E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)
taken as written
a steward serves passengers on a plane
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A cabin crew member runs out of steam after a trip to Spain, then flies on to Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thence' means from there, that is from Spain; Italy lies to the east of Spain, which is why the definition ends with a question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling from Spain to Italy means heading in the direction of sunrise, so the journey goes that way.

clue.text: Nationals chant of Russia in revolution

indicators.note: things in revolution are turned over and overthrown, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A national song sung during the Russian Revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nationals' looks like part of the surface about anthems, but it is the definition: citizens of one particular country.
explanation.definitionFit: South Africans are citizens of South Africa, so they are one country's nationals, a particular example.

clue.text: Charlie excited, having boozed it up

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
aroused means stirred up or excited

explanation.surface: Charlie is worked up after a heavy drinking session.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is the radio code word for the letter C.
explanation.definitionFit: To carouse is to drink heavily and noisily in a merry group, so both are past-tense verbs for drinking parties.

clue.text: A baron puts to sea, we're told, goes down by rock

indicators.note: what we are told reaches us by ear, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for baron
a ship that puts to sea sails; spelt here to match the German-derived word

explanation.surface: A nobleman sets sail and, reportedly, heads down past the cliffs.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is pronounced 'ab-sails', which is why the sound of sailing gives its ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Abseiling is descending a cliff or rock face on a rope, controlling the slide with the feet against the rock.

clue.text: Unimaginative writer, 'dated': that's cutting

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: a thing that cuts

blocks.note: a hack churns out dull, formulaic writing
to date someone is to see or go out with them

explanation.surface: A cutting review calls a writer boring and old-fashioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dated' wants to mean old-fashioned; it is the past tense of dating someone, as in 'she saw him for a year'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacksaw is a fine-toothed saw in a frame used for cutting through metal, a tool whose whole job is cutting.

clue.text: Familial emblem incorporating a horse and Everyman, most weather-beaten?

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take something into a body, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a family crest is a heraldic emblem
taken as written
gee-gee is a childish word for a horse
the setter refers to themself, so I

explanation.surface: A family coat of arms featuring a horse and the setter, looking very worn.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming themself (here Everyman) means I or ME. GG is the nursery word gee-gee.
explanation.definitionFit: A craggy face is rugged and deeply lined, as weathered skin is; the question mark flags this extended sense.

clue.text: Game play

blocks.note: first meaning: a board game with black-and-white discs
second meaning: a Shakespeare tragedy

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like one idea, as in 'game play', but each is a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a disc-flipping strategy board game, also called Reversi, and to Shakespeare's tragedy of the jealous Moor.

clue.text: Judicial investigation making sense

blocks.note: first meaning: a session where a case is heard in court
second meaning: one of the five senses

explanation.surface: A court inquiry that finally makes sense of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making sense' reads as an idiom; split it, and 'sense' alone is the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a formal legal session before a judge and the faculty of perceiving sound with the ears.

clue.text: Fizzy cocktail in can

blocks.note: first meaning: tequila and a fizzy mixer, banged on the table before drinking
second meaning: slang for prison

explanation.surface: A sparkling cocktail sold in a tin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' suggests a drinks tin; it is American slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: A slammer is a drink of tequila and a fizzy mixer, and also slang for jail, like can.

clue.text: Ones going through exams with felt tips

blocks.note: first meaning: examiners who grade papers
second meaning: pens with felt nibs

explanation.surface: Students sitting exams armed with coloured felt-tip pens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going through exams' suggests candidates taking them, but it means examiners working through the scripts.
explanation.definitionFit: Examiners who grade scripts are called this, and so are thick felt-tipped pens used for highlighting or labelling.

clue.text: Gossip: purveyor of beachwear catching cold?

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so one piece closes around another

blocks.note: a seller of sandals, with monger meaning trader as in fishmonger
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Rumour has it the beach-shoe seller has caught a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: Monger is an old word for a dealer, still seen in fishmonger and ironmonger.
explanation.definitionFit: A scandalmonger spreads malicious rumours about others, so the noun gossip, meaning such a person, fits.

clue.text: Greek character, one down in the mouth?

blocks.note: first meaning: the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet
second meaning: land built up at a river's mouth, downstream

explanation.surface: A gloomy figure from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down in the mouth' means miserable, but read literally it is the silt-built land lying downstream at a river's mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The fourth Greek letter shares its name with the fan of sediment at a river mouth, named for the triangular letter shape.

clue.text: Verbally make fun of golfers' items

indicators.note: verbally means spoken out loud, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: to make fun of someone is to tease them

explanation.surface: Mocking golfers about their kit, to their faces.
explanation.walkthrough: The spoken word for mocking sounds exactly like the plural of the golf peg.
explanation.definitionFit: A tee is the small peg on which a golfer places the ball before driving it.

clue.text: Homo sapiens leaving baboon to find tool

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: the mandrill is a colourful baboon
the scientific name for the human species

explanation.surface: Evolution: humans part ways with apes and discover tools.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark the Latin species name, which simply means man.
explanation.definitionFit: A drill is a tool for boring holes, and also happens to be the name of another baboon species.

clue.text: 007's adventure: duck!

blocks.note: first meaning: a James Bond film
second meaning: a diving sea duck

explanation.surface: An action scene where James Bond yells at someone to get down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck!' reads as a shouted warning to dodge; it is the bird. Ian Fleming named his Jamaican house after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1995 Bond film shares its name with a diving duck noted for its yellow eyes.

clue.text: Horrified, as some windbag has telephoned

indicators.note: some means a part of the whole, so a run of consecutive letters is taken from the words

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: Appalled because a long-winded bore has phoned yet again.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the word boundaries, starting near the end of the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aghast means filled with shock and dismay, a direct synonym for horrified.

clue.text: Holy person unchanged, in equilibrium

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for saint
as is means in its current, unaltered state

explanation.surface: A saint who never changes, perfectly balanced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As is' is the phrase sellers use for goods offered unaltered, faults and all.
explanation.definitionFit: Stasis is a state of balance or inactivity where nothing changes, close in sense to a steady equilibrium.
